content: The control of tuberculosis (TB) is critical for public health, and it is essential to educate policymakers about the significant consequences that will arise if resources for state and local TB control programs continue to decline. Drug-resistant TB presents substantial biomedical research challenges. There are still significant gaps in our understanding of the genetics and growth characteristics of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, as well as the physiology and biochemistry of both the host and the pathogen during infection. Additionally, there is a need to identify disease markers and genotypic and biological indicators that can aid in surveillance and provide insights into infection, disease progression, and drug resistance. Basic research must be supported to address these gaps, improve diagnostic and treatment strategies, and develop new approaches. The emergence of drug-resistant TB highlights the urgent need for new and effective drug regimens to treat TB, including multidrug-resistant (MDR) TB and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB. These regimens should also aim to prevent the progression of active disease in individuals latently infected with drug-resistant M. tuberculosis. Poor adherence to therapy is a major factor contributing to the development of MDR and XDR TB. Therefore, research into behavioral and social factors is necessary to identify strategies to improve patient adherence and ensure treatment completion. There is a pressing need for new, rapid, and cost-effective diagnostic methods, particularly for use in rural areas and developing countries. Ultimately, the development of an effective vaccine is essential to eliminate TB. To effectively control XDR TB, existing partnerships must be strengthened, and new collaborations must be established between countries and within both the public and private sectors. These partnerships should include government and non-government organizations. They are necessary to focus resources on the most affected geographic areas, increase financial and human resources, coordinate efforts (including research, education, laboratory, and programmatic activities), and raise awareness of the problem and its consequences. Comprehensive information on the cost of treating and implementing programs to prevent XDR TB is currently lacking. Research is needed to evaluate the cost-effectiveness and benefits of interventions and strategies to combat XDR TB. Laboratories play a critical role in diagnosing and managing drug-resistant TB. Test results must be available promptly to enable clinicians to make timely decisions regarding patient management. However, many laboratory techniques used to confirm TB diagnoses and identify drug resistance were developed decades ago, in the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s. While significant advancements in culture techniques and rapid diagnostic methods have been made in the past decade, these improved methods have not been widely implemented, especially in regions where MDR and XDR TB are prevalent. Optimized algorithms for rapid, point-of-care laboratory confirmation of TB and detection of drug resistance have not yet been established. To address the growing problem of TB drug resistance, the most current diagnostic methods must be fully utilized, and better diagnostic tests must be developed. The needs of TB laboratories must be addressed to make diagnostic services for TB, MDR TB, and XDR TB more rapid, sensitive, reliable, and responsive to the requirements of patient management, infection control, and TB control efforts. Although challenges and potential solutions vary by setting, both domestic and international TB laboratories face many of the same issues. Many clinicians, laboratorians, healthcare professionals, public health officials, and policymakers lack up-to-date knowledge about appropriate laboratory capabilities and the proper use of diagnostic tests to achieve prompt and accurate TB diagnoses. It is essential to increase awareness of the need to develop the necessary capacity and capabilities for laboratory diagnosis of TB. This includes the proper use of diagnostic tests, timely reporting of results, and accurate interpretation of test results to establish a definitive diagnosis and guide TB management, both domestically and internationally. The quality and proficiency of TB laboratory diagnosis vary within the United States and internationally due to the lack of a universally well-trained and stable laboratory workforce. In certain local public health laboratories, TB diagnostic services are limited and often rely on networks of other public and private laboratories with better diagnostic capabilities. This dependency frequently results in substantial delays in TB diagnosis and treatment. A systems-based approach is needed to improve TB laboratory services at the local level. This includes assessing the availability and capacity of TB laboratory services within a jurisdiction to identify unmet needs, obstacles to accessing services, and opportunities for improvement. Additionally, the actual costs of providing TB laboratory services through existing programs should be evaluated, and a business plan should be developed to deliver these services through an integrated system of laboratory services in the United States.
